headline: Slow growth, sticky rates, creeping debt: a world patched together, never fixed

events: US extends sectoral tariffs to pharma inputs and legacy chips; China answers with tighter rare-earth and battery-material licensing
Ukraine front freezes into a de facto ceasefire line without a peace treaty; European defence budgets keep rising toward 3% of GDP
Fed trims to ~3.25% then pauses as core inflation sticks near 3%; ECB holds at 2%
Ethiopia-style restructurings drag on; Senegal and Bolivia enter IMF programmes
AI capex boom continues but data-centre power constraints delay projects in the US Midwest and Ireland
US presidential election produces divided government; tariff regime survives the transition largely intact
Mild AI-equity correction (~20%) as hyperscaler revenue lags capex; no systemic credit event, but private-credit marks slip
Bond-market wobble: US 10-year touches 5.4% after a weak Treasury auction; Japan's JGB yields hit post-1990s highs, BoJ slows QT
Bolivia defaults; Pakistan and Egypt roll over debt only with Gulf and Chinese bridge loans
Record heat summer in South Asia; India accelerates solar-plus-storage tenders
Global growth dips to ~2.3%; global unemployment peaks near 5.6% as white-collar hiring freezes and AI-driven back-office cuts concentrate in services
EU adopts CBAM phase-in fully and a joint defence-bond facility; Chinese EV tariffs replaced by local-content deals
Armed border clash between two Sahel states escalates into sustained conflict, worsening migration flows toward North Africa and Europe
China announces another local-government debt swap; growth officially ~4%, true pace lower
Second wave of Global South distress: Kenya and Laos restructure under the G20 Common Framework
COP35 confirms 2030 NDC targets missed; global emissions edge down only ~1% from peak
US deficit stays near 7% of GDP; interest costs exceed defence spending for the third year
Housing protests and rent-control ballot wins in several European and Canadian cities
Agentic AI tools reach mid-sized firms; productivity gains visible in software, finance and logistics but not in aggregate GDP statistics
WTO dispute system remains paralysed; plurilateral 'minilateral' trade clubs proliferate
G20 inflation settles near 3%; policy rates plateau at 3-3.5%, well above pre-2020 norms
France forced into a fiscal consolidation package after a ratings downgrade and spread spike, ECB TPI not activated
Middle East conflict persists at lower intensity; shipping through Red Sea partially normalised with insurance premia elevated
Renewables pass 40% of global electricity; coal use in China declines for a second year
Populist parties enter or lead governments in three more OECD countries, mostly on cost-of-living and migration platforms

winners: India and Vietnam as 'connector' economies absorbing supply-chain diversion
Gulf states as financiers, energy suppliers and swing diplomatic brokers
Large AI and cloud platforms plus grid and power-equipment makers
losers: Indebted low-income countries in Africa facing aid cuts and high refinancing costs
Young renters and entry-level white-collar workers in rich economies
Export-dependent mid-sized manufacturers in Germany and Northeast Asia caught between blocs
bullets: World growth averaged ~2.7%, below the pre-pandemic trend; no global recession, but no boom either.
Public debt crept past 100% of world GDP as interest bills, defence and ageing costs crowded out investment.
Real interest rates stayed positive and policy rates settled around 3-3.5%, making fiscal arithmetic steadily harder.
Trade has hardened into overlapping blocs and club deals; tariffs are higher than in 2026 but not prohibitive.
AI is now used by roughly a third of firms; it has quietly thinned junior office jobs while aggregate productivity gains remain modest.
Four sovereign debt crises hit frontier economies, handled slowly through ad hoc rescues rather than a new debt architecture.
Renewables reach ~43% of electricity, yet warming is on track to breach 1.6C around 2033.
Trust keeps eroding and protests over rents and living costs are routine, but democracies bend rather than break.
wildcard: A weak US Treasury auction in 2028 briefly pushed 10-year yields to 5.4%, forcing a coordinated Fed-Treasury buyback reassurance.
image_description: In a hot 2031 Lagos evening, a young graduate waits under a solar-powered bus shelter, scrolling an AI job-matching app that keeps offering gig translation work, while a tariff-priced Chinese e-scooter hums past a half-finished data centre.
